toolkits.name: Integrated Gradients (IG)

description.overview: Integrated Gradients (IG) attributes predictions to input tokens by integrating gradients along a path from a baseline to the actual input.
main_functionalities: Compute token-level attribution scores relative to a baseline

strengths: Satisfies axioms of sensitivity and implementation invariance
More stable and less noisy than raw gradients
Support configurable number of integration steps
Provides intuitive baseline comparison ('change from reference to input')
limitations: Requires choosing a baseline, which affects results
Computationally expensive due to multiple forward/backward passes
Can provide noisy explanations

toolkits.name: Layer Integrated Gradients

description.overview: Layer Integrated Gradients is a variation of Integrated Gradients that computes importance scores for the inputs or outputs of a specific layer, rather than for the original input features. In contrast, Integrated Gradients assigns an importance score to each input feature by approximating the integral of the gradients of the model’s output with respect to those inputs along a path from chosen reference inputs to the actual inputs.
main_functionalities: Compute attributions for internal layer inputs or outputs
Enable analysis of intermediate representations in addition to providing local attribution scores

strengths: Like Integrated Gradients, provides theoretically grounded attributions satisfying axioms
Enables interpretability of intermediate representations rather than input features
More stable than raw gradient-based methods due to path integration
Can be combined with token-level for finer-grained inspection
limitations: Like Integrated Gradients, sensitive to the choice of baseline/reference input
Like Integrated Gradients, it can be computationally expensive

toolkits.name: Saliency

description.overview: Saliency attributes predictions to input tokens by computing the gradient of the output with respect to the input.
main_functionalities: Compute token-level attribution scores

strengths: Very fast (single forward pass)
Easy to interpret as 'which tokens influence the output most'

Admits an intuitive interpretation as the first-order Taylor approximation of the model around the input. The gradients represent the coefficients of this local linear approximation, and their magnitude is used as a measure of how sensitive the prediction is to each input token.
Useful for quick debugging and visualization
limitations: Often noisy or unstable, prone to highlight spurious importances
Suffers from gradient saturation, which means that gradients approach zero and can be misleading in a neighbourhood of the inputs
Small changes in the input around thresholds imposed by nonlinearities in the transformer computations can lead to large jumps in gradient-based attribution scores
Does not satisfy desirable axioms like sensitivity and implementation invariance

toolkits.name: DeepLift

description.overview: DeepLIFT attributes the change in output to differences in input relative to a chosen baseline by backpropagating activation differences using specific propagation rules.

strengths: Often faster than Integrated Gradients
Handles cases of zero gradients (saturation) more robustly than raw-gradient tools
It satisfies the summation-to-delta property, a desirable property similar to completeness for Integrated Gradients

description.overview: GradientSHAP combines integrated gradients with randomized baselines to approximate Shapley-value attributions via gradient estimates.

description.overview: Occlusion masks out contiguous input segments (e.g., spans of tokens) and measures the effect on model output. The difference indicates the importance of the occluded region.

toolkits.name: Shapley Value Sampling

description.overview: Shapley Value Sampling approximates SHAP attributions by Monte Carlo sampling of feature coalitions, averaging each feature's marginal contribution to the model's prediction across sampled subsets.

strengths: Game-theoretic foundation (Shapley values)
Model-agnostic (no gradients required)
Very popular across different domains
limitations: Can be very expensive; stable estimates often require many samples
Perturbations/masking can create out-of-distribution inputs

toolkits.name: TokenSHAP

description.overview: TokenSHAP adapts Shapley values from cooperative game theory to attribute importance scores to individual tokens or substrings in an input prompt. It uses and ad-hoc Monte Carlo sampling strategy for computational efficiency.

strengths: Theoretically grounded in game theory
Tailored to autoregressive LLMs (explains next-token or sequence probabilities)
Human friendly explanations
limitations: Computationally expensive
Results depend on masking/perturbation strategy, which may create out-of-distribution inputs
Shapley values approximation may be unstable if enough Monte Carlo samples are not drawn

toolkits.name: Leave-One-Out (LOO) / Erasure

description.overview: Leave-One-Out attribution estimates the importance of each input token by removing it one at a time and measuring the change in the model's likelihood for a target continuation. It is the special case of Captum's FeatureAblation with no feature grouping, and serves as a natural baseline for more sophisticated perturbation-based methods such as SHAP.
main_functionalities: Compute per-token importance for a target generated continuation by single-token ablation

strengths: Simple and intuitive: directly measures the effect of removing each token
Model-agnostic (only requires forward passes)
Serves as the conceptual baseline for many other perturbation-based attribution methods
limitations: Cost scales linearly with input length (one forward pass per token)
Removing a single token can create out-of-distribution inputs
Ignores interaction effects between tokens (unlike Shapley-based methods)

toolkits.name: SmoothGrad

description.overview: Instead of using raw gradients to compute attributions, which can be unstable, SmoothGrad approximates a smoothing of the raw gradients based on a Gaussian kernel.
main_functionalities: Compute token-level attribution scores

strengths: More stable than attribution tools based on raw gradients
Reduces visual artifacts and sharp discontinuities in attributions, leading to explanations that are easier to interpret
Can be viewed as a general procedure which computes an attribution map by averaging over multiple attribution maps of an arbitrary gradient-based attribution method with multiple noised input
limitations: More computationally demanding than attribution tools based on raw gradients, requiring multiple forward passes
Obtaining proper results requires carefully selecting the variance of the Gaussian noise
Not tailored to natural language

toolkits.name: Direct Logit Attribution

description.overview: Direct Logit Attribution (DLA) projects the contribution of each model component to the logit space contribution onto a target token logit. Positive contributions push the logit up (toward the token), negatives push it down.
main_functionalities: Compute signed contributions of model components to a chosen next-token prediction

strengths: Fast and simple: one forward pass plus linear projections
Intuitive signed contributions (direct evidence vs. counter-evidence)
Helps locate where the prediction is being written in the model
limitations: Not causal: large contribution might be erased later
Ignores possibile interactions (softmax competition, nonlinear effects)
Depends on normalization placement (affects interpretability)

toolkits.name: Logit Lens

description.overview: Logit Lens projects each intermediate hidden state through the model’s output head to view predicted token probabilities at each layer. It tracks how the model’s top prediction evolves through the layers.

strengths: Very fast: one forward pass provides layer-wise outputs
Shows when and how representations become linearly decodable
Natural for decoder-only LMs (no additional sampling)
limitations: Not causal: reveals decode-ability, not true necessity
Intermediate states require proper normalization for comparison
Top-k outputs can be misleading when probabilities are diffuse

toolkits.name: Probing

description.overview: Probing assesses what information is encoded in a model’s internal representations by training simple, and often linear, classifiers (or probes) on internal representations.
main_functionalities: Measures whether specific linguistic or semantic properties can be decoded at a certain location within the transformer

strengths: Probing is fast and easy-to-implement, given a dataset of activations
Allows to test hypotheses on what information the model has stored in different locations
Can uncover interesting directions in the activation space, paving the way for activation steering
limitations: Even if some information is decodable at a certain location, it does not mean that it is used for prediction
The results are affected by the learning capabilities of the probe. The choice of the classifier is not obvious
The property to probe for must be predetermined
Training the probe requires a labeled dataset

toolkits.name: Attention Rollout

description.overview: Attention Rollout accounts for the full flow of information through a transformer by recursively multiplying attention matrices across layers. This produces a single aggregated attention score for any pair of tokens, capturing indirect dependencies that single-layer attention weights miss.
main_functionalities: Aggregate attention weights across heads and layers
Compute token-to-token relevance scores

strengths: Efficient: uses existing attention weights (no backprop required)
Intuitive:  at the implementation level, the method boils down to multiplying attention matrices across layers.
Provides intuitive visualization of attention dependencies
limitations: Inherits the lack of faithfulness of attention-based explanations (attention may not reflect true importance)

toolkits.name: Attention Flow

description.overview: Leveraging flow-network ideas from graph theory, Attention Flow represents tokens across transformer layers as nodes connected by attention-weighted edges and estimates token-to-token influence by computing maximum flow through this layered network.
main_functionalities: Aggregate attention weights across heads and layers
Compute token-to-token relevance scores

strengths: Theoretically grounded in graph theory
Accounts for multiple possible attention paths across layers
Does not require gradients or model re-evaluation
limitations: Inherits the lack of faithfulness of attention-based explanations (attention may not reflect true importance)

toolkits.name: Aggregation of Layer-wise Token-to-token Interactions (ALTI)

description.overview: ALTI quantifies how contextual information is mixed across transformer layers by modeling token-to-token interactions within each attention block and aggregating them to produce attribution scores.
main_functionalities: Quantifies token-to-token interaction within each layer
Computes token-level local attribution scores

strengths: Models the full attention block rather than relying on attention weights alone
It can provide more robust and faithful explanations than baselines such as Integrated Gradients and Attention Rollout
limitations: Assumes that attention can be used as an explanation
Ignores MLPs
Ignores the classifier on top of the transformer and hence cannot provide explanations for each of the output classes

toolkits.name: LIT Counterfactual Generator

description.overview: The tool supports counterfactual generation techniques to provide behavioral analysis through systematic input manipulation. The idea is to create modified versions of the original input by substituting, removing, or adding tokens and then observing how the model's predictions change in response to these perturbations. main_functionalities: Generate counterfactual examples for a given input
Show the differences needed to alter the predictions of the model

strengths: Explanations are intuitive
The method is model agnostic
limitations: The unit (or subset of input) that can be targeted to generate a counterfactual is not obvious
Different approaches to counterfactual generation can be more or less effective

description.overview: Polyjuice is a transformer-based counterfactual generation framework. It uses a fine-tuned GPT-2 model with perturbation control codes to generate fluent and diverse textual variants of an input. These counterfactuals are evaluated on a target classifier to analyze prediction changes.

Show the differences needed to alter the predictions of the model

The method is model agnostic
Explanations are intuitive

Not classifier-aware: counterfactuals are generated without guidance from the target classifier decision boundary
The control codes used to guide generation and fine-tuning may be subject to biases

toolkits.name: Activation Patching

description.overview: Activation patching studies which components of a model are responsible for a behavior by replacing internal activations. In particular, activations from a “clean” run are copied into a “corrupted” run (or vice-versa) to assess the impact of the intervention
main_functionalities: Identify computational paths that are important for a behavior of the model of interest
Identify critical components

strengths: Allows to draw strong causal conclusions
Allows localizing precise model components affecting a behavior
limitations: Requires manual work, e.g., to creation of a dataset of corrupted inputs to collect activations from the “corrupted” run
Patching interventions are computationally expensive, requiring multiple passes
Results are affected by design choices such as the creation of corrupted inputs or the chouce of the metric used to assess patching impact
