research_applications.note: Evaluates the impact of design choices in activation patching, providing recommendations for the best practices of activation patching going forwards.

toolkits.name: Path Patching

description.overview: Path patching is a causal intervention method where activations from a “clean” run are copied into a “corrupted” run (or vice-versa), but only along a specific computational path to test whether that precise path is responsible for a given behavior or prediction.
main_functionalities: Identify computational paths that are important for a behavior of the model of interest
Localize important and unimportant computational subgraphs

strengths: Allows to draw strong causal conclusions
Computational paths are not always easy-to-interpret for humans
Allows to study which transformer components affect each other directly, or via mediation by another component
More expressive than standard activation patching
limitations: Requires manual work, e.g., to creation of a dataset of corrupted inputs to collect activations from the “corrupted” run
Patching interventions are computationally expensive, requiring multiple passes
Results are affected by design choices such as the creation of corrupted inputs or the choice of the metric used to assess patching impact

research_applications.used_in: Interpretability in the wild: a circuit for indirect object identification in gpt-2 small
research_applications.note: Introduces path-constrained activation patching.

research_applications.used_in: Localizing model behavior with path patching
research_applications.note: Introduces path-constrained activation patching.

research_applications.used_in: How to use and interpret activation patching
research_applications.note: Exhaustively illustrates activation patching, also covering path patching.

toolkits.name: Attribution Patching (AtP) and AtP*

description.overview: Attribution Patching (AtP) is a fast, gradient-based first-order approximation to activation patching: it estimates the effect of patching an activation by computing the inner product between the activation difference (clean−corrupted) and the gradient of a behavior metric with respect to that activation. AtP* is a refined variant designed to reduce the approximation quality of AtP in attention-saturated and cancellation-heavy settings while preserving scalability.
main_functionalities: Efficiently compute an importance score per component (e.g., attention head or MLP) which approximates causal activation patching

strengths: Scalable and efficient

As an approximation of the expensive but causal and reliable activation patching, AtP can serve as a *pre-filter* to focus expensive causal interventions (activation/path patching) on a small candidate set
Can be useful to discover small computational subgraphs responsible for a given behavior (i.e., circuits)
limitations: Approximate, not strictly causal: it is a local linearization and can disagree with true activation patching when effects are highly non-linear or large, particularly for standard AtP
Still sensitive to experimental design (construction of clean and corrupted dataset, choice of metric and choice of granularity for the computational graph)

AtP* improves the approximation of activation patching with respect to AtP, but adds extra implementation complexity (attention-specific handling + cancellation mitigation) and may be harder to generalize

research_applications.used_in: Attribution patching: activation patching at industrial scale
research_applications.note: Introduces AtP as a first-order Taylor approximation to activation patching and motivates it as a scalable heuristic.

research_applications.used_in: AtP*: Efficient and scalable methods for localizing LLM behaviour to components
research_applications.note: Studies failure modes of AtP and subsequently introduces AtP* improvements (attention saturation + cancellation), plus diagnostics for remaining false negatives.

toolkits.name: Edge Attribution Patching with Integrated Gradients (EAP-IG)

description.overview: EAP-IG is a gradient-based circuit-discovery method that scores the causal importance of every edge (connection between attention heads and MLPs) in a transformer's computational graph using a small, fixed number of forward and backward passes. It extends Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) by averaging the loss gradient over several points along a straight-line interpolation between a clean and a corrupted input's activations (as in Integrated Gradients), instead of evaluating the gradient only at the clean input.
main_functionalities: Computes an importance (attribution) score for every edge in a transformer's computational graph in a few forward/backward passes (default m=5 interpolation steps)
Mitigates EAP's 'zero-gradient' failure mode, where an important edge can be scored as unimportant because the gradient happens to be flat at the clean input
Supports arbitrary task metrics converted to a loss, including KL divergence between the patched and unpatched output distributions
Feeds a scored edge graph into a downstream circuit-selection step (thresholding or greedy edge selection) that yields a discrete sparse circuit

strengths: Mitigates the zero/near-zero gradient problem that affects plain EAP by sampling gradients at multiple interpolated points instead of one
Produces circuits that are as faithful as, or more faithful than, plain EAP circuits across most tested tasks
Needs only a few interpolation steps (m=5, sometimes m=3) to work well, so overhead over plain EAP is modest
Enables use of KL divergence as a universal loss, which is unusable with plain EAP because its single-point gradient collapses to zero under KL at the clean input
Edge-importance rankings correlate better with true activation-patching scores than EAP's rankings do

Adopted in later large-scale studies (e.g., tracking circuits across training and model scale) specifically for its faithful circuit-finding ability, and reported as the strongest single baseline in the MIB shared task on circuit localization
limitations: Does not consistently reduce absolute approximation error relative to true activation-patching scores compared to plain EAP
Its fixed, model-agnostic straight-line interpolation path still passes through regions of near-zero gradient (a 'saturation effect'), which a follow-up method (EAP-GP) was designed to address
Can find a circuit that is faithful at the cost of omitting important components with negative (inhibitory) contributions, so faithfulness alone does not guarantee completeness

As a gradient-based estimator it amplifies the intrinsic statistical variance of single-input causal-mediation scores, making discovered circuits sensitive to bootstrap resampling of the input dataset and to hyperparameter/aggregation choices, especially in larger models
Circuits can shift substantially when the same task is rephrased with different templates or when the probing dataset is resampled from the same distribution
About 5x slower than plain EAP, since it requires a gradient computation at each of the m interpolation steps

research_applications.used_in: Have Faith in Faithfulness: Going Beyond Circuit Overlap When Finding Model Mechanisms
research_applications.note: Introduces EAP-IG.

research_applications.used_in: EAP-GP: Mitigating Saturation Effect in Gradient-based Automated Circuit Identification
research_applications.note: Identifies a 'saturation effect' in EAP-IG's fixed straight-line interpolation path and proposes EAP-GP, a model-dependent interpolation path that outperforms EAP-IG on faithfulness and precision/recall at higher runtime cost.

research_applications.used_in: Mechanistic Interpretability as Statistical Estimation: A Variance Analysis of EAP-IG
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)
research_applications.note: Analyzes EAP-IG as an approximate estimator of causal mediation analysis, showing it amplifies per-input variance and that resulting circuits are unstable under data resampling and hyperparameter choices.

research_applications.used_in: Demystifying Variance in Circuit Discovery of LLMs
research_applications.note: Calls EAP-IG the state-of-the-art faithfulness method but documents resampling and template-rephrasing variance in its circuits, and proves its integrated-gradients scoring rule violates 'additive order preservation'.

research_applications.used_in: LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the 38th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
research_applications.note: Adopts EAP-IG as the circuit-finding method of choice to track circuit emergence and stability across 300B tokens of Pythia training and multiple model scales.

research_applications.used_in: BlackboxNLP-2025 MIB Shared Task: Exploring Ensemble Strategies for Circuit Localization Methods
research_applications.note: Reports EAP-IG (on input attributions) as the strongest single baseline method in the MIB circuit-localization shared task, and uses it to warm-start a more expensive ensembling approach.

research_applications.used_in: PATCH: Mitigating PII Leakage in Language Models with Privacy-Aware Targeted Circuit PatcHing
research_applications.source: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EACL 2026
research_applications.note: Applies EAP-IG as the circuit-discovery mechanism to identify circuits responsible for PII leakage in fine-tuned language models, then edits those circuits to reduce leakage.

toolkits.name: Minimal Contrastive Editing (MICE)

description.overview: Minimal Contrastive Editing (MICE) explains a model prediction by generating minimally edited versions of an input text that flip the model’s prediction. The method works in two stages: first an editor model is trained to propose edits targeting the predictor’s output; then these edits are used to generate contrastive examples, from which the smallest change that alters the prediction is identified.
main_functionalities: Generate counterfactual inputs close to the original inputs that flip the model prediction

strengths: Produces intuitive explanations by identifying limited edits to the input that alter the output
limitations: Can be very computationally expensive, requiring fine-tuning and multiple passes
Quality of explanations depends on the editing model used to generate candidate changes
Edits may produce slightly unnatural or semantically altered sentences

research_applications.used_in: Explaining NLP Models via Minimal Contrastive Editing (MICE)
research_applications.source: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics
research_applications.note: Introduces the MICE method for generating minimal contrastive edits that explain NLP model predictions.

toolkits.name: MLP Update Decomposition

description.overview: This method decomposes a Transformer MLP (feed-forward) layer as updates that pertain to single paramter vectors. Each vector is then projected to the vocabulary space and interpreted as promoting specific concepts.
main_functionalities: Decompose the MLP update into components which can be interpreted

strengths: Valuable to gain fine-grained insight on the mechanisms implemented in the MLP, which is a core yet poorly-understood component of the transformer.
Vectors in the decomposition of the MLP update are often interpretable.
Allows steering generation towards a direction of interest
limitations: Possible non-linear interactions between MLP weight vectors that may generate new meanings are ignored.

research_applications.used_in: Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Build Predictions by Promoting Concepts in the Vocabulary Space
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the 2022 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
research_applications.note: Introduces vocabulary-space FFN decomposition.

research_applications.used_in: LM-Debugger: An Interactive Tool for Inspection and Intervention in Transformer-Based Language Models
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the 2022 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing: System Demonstrations
research_applications.note: Uses vocabulary-space analysis for debugging transformers and intervening to steer their outputs.

toolkits.name: Training Data Influence (TracIn)

description.overview: Estimates the influence of a training example on a specific test prediction by approximating how stochastic gradient descent updates changed the test loss during training. Concretely, at multiple saved training checkpoints, it computes the dot product between the gradient of the loss on the training example and the gradient of the loss on the test example, and sums these gradient-alignment scores (weighted by the learning rate) across checkpoints.
main_functionalities: Compute training data attribution (or influence) scores
Influence can be computed on all model parameters or restricted to selected layers (e.g., only the final layer) to reduce computational cost and memory usage.

strengths: Scalable and efficient
Useful for dataset debugging
limitations: Results can be noisy and depend on design choices (checkpoints, target layers, and the loss/target used)

research_applications.used_in: Estimating training data influence by tracing gradient descent
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
research_applications.note: Introduces TracIn.

research_applications.used_in: TracIn: A simple method to estimate training data influence
research_applications.note: High-level explanation and intuition for gradient-alignment influence scores.

research_applications.used_in: Analyzing the use of influence functions for instance-specific data filtering in leural machine translation
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the Seventh Conference on Machine Translation
research_applications.note: Applies TracIn to neural machine translation.

toolkits.name: Attention Visualization (BertViz)

description.overview: BertViz is a tool for visualizing self-attention in transformers at multiple scales. It provides views of individual heads, all heads, or neuron-level interactions.
main_functionalities: Visualize attention patterns between tokens across layers and heads
Provide multiple interactive views (head-level, model-level)

strengths: Easy to access
Intuitive visualizations
Can focus on a specific attention head or provide a complete view of all attention heads in the model
limitations: Attention is known not to provide faithful explananations (see "Attention is not Explanation" in Further Readings section)

research_applications.used_in: A Multiscale Visualization of Attention in the Transformer Model
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the 57th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics: System Demonstrations
research_applications.note: Introduces BertViz tool and its views.

toolkits.name: exBERT

description.overview: exBERT (available at: https://exbert.vizhub.ai/client/exBERT.html) is a tool which provides a concise overview of attention (attention view) and the internal representations (corpus view).
main_functionalities: Visualize attention weights and token embeddings for a given input
Computes summary statistics summarizing internal representations for a given token

strengths: Useful to quickly test hypotheses on the internal representation of a specific token in a specific context
The tool can be easily accessed online at https://exbert.vizhub.ai/client/exBERT.html
limitations: Attention is known not to provide faithful explanations (see "Attention is not Explanation" in Further Readings section)
exBERT only provides statistics for a single token, considering a small number of neighbours, yielding no insights on global behaviors

research_applications.used_in: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics: System Demonstrations
research_applications.note: Presents exBERT interactive tool.

research_applications.used_in: Attention is not Explanation
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the 2019 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies, Volume 1
research_applications.note: Finds that attention patterns do not provide faithful explanations.

toolkits.name: Sparse Autoencoders

description.overview: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) train a larger, sparse latent space to reconstruct model interal representations (activations) with the goal of disentangling highly-polysemantic features into more monosemantic features. Each sparse unit aims to capture a semantically meaningful concept.
main_functionalities: Enable discovery of human-interpretable features
Facilitates investigation of the causal role of discovered features via ablation

strengths: Allows discovery of latent feature directions without supervision
Often effectively yields more monosemantic features than raw neurons
Integrates with any model layer for interpretability
limitations: Interpreting meaning of discovered features is not straightforward and may require human inspection (e.g., via top activations)
No guarantee of true monosemantics; polysemantic features may remain
In training, there is a trade-off between reconstruction quality and sparsity

research_applications.used_in: Sparse autoencoders find highly interpretable features in language models
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR)
research_applications.note: Empirically demonstrates that SAEs trained on language model activations yield highly interpretable and monosemantic features.

research_applications.used_in: Towards monosemanticity: decomposing language models with dictionary learning
research_applications.note: Introduces large-scale SAEs for discovering monosemantic features.

research_applications.used_in: Toy models of superposition
research_applications.note: Explains the superposition hypothesis and role of sparse features.

research_applications.used_in: Neuronpedia
research_applications.note: Neuronpedia is a platform for exploring and interpreting internal features of neural networks by visualizing Sparse Autoencoders (SAE) features, showing where those learned directions in model activations fire and what patterns or concepts they represent.

toolkits.name: Transcoders

description.overview: Transcoders replace MLP sublayers in a transformer with a sparse, interpretable approximation: a wide feed-forward network with a sparse bottleneck trained to mimic the original MLP's input-output behavior. Each feature in the bottleneck can be interpreted as a localized, human-readable computation. Unlike Sparse Autoencoders, which reconstruct activations, transcoders learn to approximate the MLP's functional mapping from input to output.
main_functionalities: Enable decomposition of MLP computations into human-intrerpretable features
Support circuit-level analysis by providing a sparse computational graph over transcoder features

strengths: Find circuits  that neatly factorize into input-dependent and input-invariant term
Can give smaller circuits than Sparse Autoencoders
limitations: Introduces an approximation error: the transcoder does not perfectly replicate the original MLP, which can limit the faithfulness of derived explanations (there is a trade-off between sparsity and approximation quality)
Training transcoders for large models is computationally expensive
Interpreting transcoder features still requires human inspection (e.g., via top activations), like for Sparse Autoencoders

research_applications.used_in: Transcoders Find Interpretable LLM Feature Circuits
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the 38th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
research_applications.note: Introduces transcoders as sparse, interpretable replacements for MLP sublayers and demonstrates their use for circuit-level analysis in transformer language models.

toolkits.name: Information Flow Routes

description.overview: Given a representation of a transformer as a computational graph, Information Flow Routes identifies a sparse computational subgraph that explains a model prediction. To this aim, it computes attributions for intermediate components and prunes low-contribution edges to reveal key information pathways.
main_functionalities: Efficiently compute contributions of model components in one forward pass
Extract prediction-specific important computational subgraphs (circuits) without costly interventions

strengths: Scalable: it runs in a single pass to find circuits efficiently
No need for custom corruption or extensive patching
Highlights likely critical components for a prediction
limitations: Correlational: not strictly causal
Results depend on thresholding choices and greedy pruning
Might miss alternate pathways or subtle effects

research_applications.used_in: Information Flow Routes: Automatically Interpreting Language Models at Scale
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the 2024 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
research_applications.note: Introduces the Information Flow Routes technique.

research_applications.used_in: LM Transparency Tool: Interactive Tool for Analyzing Transformer Language Models
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 3: System Demonstrations)
research_applications.note: Presents a user interface leveraging Information Flow Routes.

toolkits.name: Automatic Circuit DisCovery (ACDC)

description.overview: Automatizes part of the workflow carried out to discover circuits responsible for a given task. In particular, researchers and practitioners are required to specify a metric describing the behavior of interest, a dataset of clean and corrupted inputs associated to the behavior of interest and the computational graph granularity ( (e.g. attention heads and MLP layers or individual neurons). Then, ACDC automatically uses patching to extract a subgraph (circuit) that is as concise as possibile while retaining the behavior of interest
main_functionalities: Given a metric describing a behavior of interest, a clean and corrupted dataset and a representation of a transformer as a computational graph, ACDC uses patching to extract concise computational subgraphs (circuits) that are causally responsibile for the behavior of interest

strengths: ACDC uses patching leads to strong causal explanations
limitations: Computationally expensive
Only automatizes part of the circuit-discovery workflow (still requires defining a metric, a corrupted dataset and the level of granularity of the computational graph)
Extracted circuits are not necessarily generalizable across models

research_applications.used_in: Towards Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability
research_applications.source: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36: Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2023)
research_applications.note: Presents the ACDC method.

toolkits.name: Edge Pruning

description.overview: Edge Pruning frames automated circuit discovery as a gradient-based optimization problem. It freezes the model's weights and learns a continuous relaxed binary mask (via the hard-concrete distribution and an L0-regularized Lagrangian sparsity objective) on every edge between components, using a modified 'disentangled residual stream' so each node can read a learned interpolation between clean and corrupted (counterfactual) activations. Thresholding the trained masks at the end yields a discrete sparse circuit.
main_functionalities: Learns continuous edge masks (and a secondary node-activity mask to speed convergence to high sparsity) via gradient descent with L0/Lagrangian sparsity control
Replaces missing edges with counterfactual (corrupted-example) activations via interchange ablation, framing edge removal as a causal intervention
Produces one discrete edge-subgraph ('circuit') per task after thresholding the trained masks
Scales via model/data parallelism to multi-billion-parameter models

strengths: More faithful and better task-performing circuits than ACDC and EAP on standard tasks, especially at high sparsity
Scales efficiently to large datasets: fastest and most faithful of compared methods when using 100K examples
Perfectly recovers ground-truth circuits on small Tracr-compiled toy programs with known ground truth
Demonstrated to scale to a 13B-parameter model, finding circuits with under 0.04% of edges that match full-model performance
Independently confirmed by follow-up work as the most faithful baseline among edge-level circuit-discovery methods compared
limitations: At small dataset sizes, approximation-based methods like EAP are faster than Edge Pruning
Higher GPU memory requirements than EAP/ACDC, especially at scale
Even at very high sparsity, circuits in large models can still contain hundreds of edges, making full interpretation difficult
Perfect output faithfulness does not guarantee the circuit represents the true underlying computation
Requires an architectural modification (disentangled residual stream), increasing GPU memory footprint versus regular structured pruning

Follow-up work reports it as computationally expensive relative to alternatives: one comparison found it needs about 5x more memory and 8x more wall-clock time than a node-level pruning alternative at matched settings

research_applications.used_in: Finding Transformer Circuits with Edge Pruning
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the 38th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
research_applications.note: Introduces Edge Pruning.

research_applications.used_in: Discovering Transformer Circuits via a Hybrid Attribution and Pruning Framework
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
research_applications.note: Builds on Edge Pruning by using attribution patching to pre-filter edges and then applying Edge Pruning to the narrowed subgraph, cutting its runtime by 46% while matching its faithfulness; also uses it as a direct experimental baseline.

research_applications.used_in: Multi-Granular Node Pruning for Causal Circuit Discovery
research_applications.note: Uses Edge Pruning as a primary baseline and critiques its edge-level formulation for coarse granularity, quadratic edge scaling, and memory/compute cost relative to their proposed node-level method.

toolkits.name: ModCirc

description.overview: ModCirc discovers a task-agnostic vocabulary of 'modular circuits' in an LLM. For a set of training tasks (reformatted into a common multi-choice/single-token-output format), it finds each task's significant computational subgraph via causal tracing (edge attribution patching with integrated gradients), extracts subgraphs that are reused across tasks, partitions them into smaller modular subgraphs using an RL-trained graph neural network, and generates a natural-language functional interpretation for each modular circuit with an LLM. The resulting vocabulary of modular circuits and their cached interpretations can then be reused to interpret unseen tasks without rederiving explanations from scratch.
main_functionalities: Unifies diverse language tasks into a common single-token-output format so circuit-discovery techniques apply uniformly
Identifies each task's significant computational subgraph via causal tracing (edge attribution patching + integrated gradients)
Finds reusable subgraphs shared across at least two tasks' circuits
Partitions reusable subgraphs into smaller modular circuits using an RL-trained graph neural network optimized for locality, composability, and globality
Generates a natural-language functional interpretation for each modular circuit using an LLM fed token-level activation heatmaps
Matches new tasks' circuits against the existing modular-circuit vocabulary to reuse cached interpretations

strengths: Provides cross-task, global interpretability by finding modular circuits shared across different tasks, rather than one-off task-specific circuits

Reduces the cost of circuit discovery via the EAP+IG approximation, and reduces the cost of interpretation by reusing cached functional interpretations instead of re-inspecting every node for every new task
Achieves notably higher reusability scores than tested baselines (random, frequent-random, clustering, activation-based) across several medical evaluation datasets

Demonstrated transferability: on GPT-2 Small, recovered 92% of the ground-truth Indirect Object Identification (IOI) circuit's components and 87.5% of a ground-truth acronym-detection circuit's nodes, with generated interpretations aligning with interpretations from prior manual analyses
limitations: The discovered modular-circuit vocabulary is limited by the scope and diversity of the training tasks used; functional aspects of the model not covered by those tasks may be missed
Evaluating consistency and reusability of circuits across tasks remains challenging, and current metrics may oversimplify how circuits are actually reused or adapted
The consistency criterion is not included in the RL training objective (only evaluated post hoc) because quantifying it requires costly LLM-prompting
Does not consistently outperform simpler baselines on the composability metric, due to its requirement to maintain connected partitions
Requires the target task's output to be reducible to a single token, so not all tasks are natively suitable without an LLM-based reformatting step

research_applications.used_in: Towards Global-level Mechanistic Interpretability: A Perspective of Modular Circuits of Large Language Models
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)
research_applications.note: Introduces ModCirc.

research_applications.used_in: From Circuit Evidence to Mechanistic Theory: An Inductive Logic Approach
research_applications.note: Cites ModCirc in related work as prior work moving toward global-level mechanistic interpretability through reusable modular circuits, contrasting its own approach of formalizing the representation layer itself; does not apply or extend ModCirc.

toolkits.name: IBCircuit

description.overview: IBCircuit is an end-to-end, gradient-optimized framework for discovering circuits in transformer language models based on the Information Bottleneck principle. It injects learnable-magnitude Gaussian noise into model components (attention heads, MLPs, and their inputs) via sigmoid-parameterized weights, training these weights jointly so the noised model's output stays close to the original model's output (low KL divergence) while minimizing the information retained from irrelevant components; after training, components with high learned weights (low injected noise) are thresholded into the final circuit.
main_functionalities: Formulates circuit discovery as an Information Bottleneck optimization with tractable variational bounds on mutual information between the circuit, the full model, and the task output
Parameterizes each node or edge with a learnable weight controlling a Gaussian-noise gate on its activation
Trains all weights jointly end-to-end via gradient descent, using only the original pretrained model's own output as supervision, without needing hand-designed corrupted/counterfactual data
Forms the final discrete circuit by thresholding learned weights against an adaptively determined cap on circuit size
Supports both node-level and edge-level circuit parameterization

strengths: Task-agnostic: does not require hand-designing task-specific corrupted/counterfactual data, unlike activation-patching or ACDC-style methods
Enables simultaneous, holistic gradient-based optimization of all component weights together, rather than sequential per-component intervention as in patching methods
Identifies more faithful and minimal circuits than Subnetwork Probing, ACDC, and Attribution Patching baselines on standard circuit-discovery benchmarks
Demonstrated to scale to a 1.5B-parameter model, matching or beating gradient-attribution baselines with far fewer edges

In an independent downstream evaluation (circuit-guided pruning), IBCircuit-selected components retained the large majority of base task accuracy, landing in what the evaluators call the 'faithful-and-effective corner' relative to other methods
limitations: Underperforms ACDC on tasks lacking a single clearly-defined correct output token, and specifically at very high sparsity on such tasks
Requires manual tuning of the trade-off between circuit sparsity and faithfulness to the original model
In an independent 6-algorithm comparison on canonical circuit-head recovery, scored mid-field, clearly below gradient-attribution (EAP-family) methods
Trains its noise mask in a single batch, so its activation memory footprint grows with model size, which limited the model scale used in at least one independent benchmark comparison

research_applications.used_in: IBCircuit: Towards Holistic Circuit Discovery with Information Bottleneck
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)
research_applications.note: Introduces IBCircuit.

research_applications.used_in: CircuitKIT: Circuit Discovery, Evaluation, and Application Toolkit for Mechanistic Interpretability
research_applications.note: Implements IBCircuit as a registered circuit-discovery algorithm and benchmarks it against EAP/EAP-IG/EAP-GP/ACDC/CD-T on canonical-circuit recovery, cross-model-family discovery, and downstream circuit-guided pruning, and documents its memory-scaling limitation.

toolkits.name: Discretized Integrated Gradients

description.overview: Discretized Integrated Gradients computes token-level attributions by integrating gradients along interpolation paths that respect the discrete structure of token embeddings, moving through actual embedding vectors rather than through continuous interpolations that may fall outside the embedding space.
main_functionalities: Computes token-level attribution scores

strengths: Like IG, more stable than raw gradients
Satisfies completeness, sensitivity and implementation invariance
Tailored to natural language
limitations: Baseline choice influences results
Computational cost scales with integration steps

research_applications.used_in: Discretized integrated gradients for explaining language models
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the 2021 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
research_applications.note: Introduces Discretized Integrated Gradients.

toolkits.name: PCA

description.overview: Projects token representations (input embeddings and hidden states) into a low-dimensional space using Principal Component Analysis (PCA). Choosing a 2D or 3D spaces, allows us to visualize the geometry of transformer representations across layers.
main_functionalities: Summarizing activations by finding the directions explaining the most variance in the latent space of a model
Enable effective visualization of the latent space of the model

strengths: Theoretically grounded, being guaranteed to identify the orthogonal directions of maximal variance
Provides intuitive visualization of representational geometry in high-dimensional spaces
Reveals layerwise evolution of token representations
Supports both fixed and per-layer PCA bases for flexible analysis
limitations: Captures only linear structure and may miss non-linear geometry
Can miss a lot of important information and may destroy important semantic relationship
Visualization quality depends on token count and sentence length

research_applications.used_in: Visualizing LLM Latent Space Geometry Through Dimensionality Reduction
research_applications.note: Applies PCA (and UMAP) to analyze latent state geometries and layerwise evolution in transformer models.

research_applications.used_in: Examining Structure of Word Embeddings with PCA
research_applications.source: International Conference of Text, Speech and Dialogue (TSD)
research_applications.note: Uses PCA to compare and interpret the geometric structure of word embeddings from different models.

research_applications.used_in: Learned Transformer Position Embeddings Have a Low-Dimensional Structure
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the 9th Workshop on Representation Learning for NLP (RepL4NLP)
research_applications.note: Applies PCA to analyze the dimensionality and structure of positional and word embeddings in BERT models. They find that positional embeddings have a low-dimensional structure, using only about 10% of the available dimensions.

toolkits.name: Linear CKA
toolkits.notes: Representation similarity across layers using linear CKA.

description.overview: Linear CKA (Centered Kernel Alignment) is a similarity measure that quantifies how similarly two sets of latent representations (e.g., neural network layer activations) encode information by comparing their centered linear kernels in a way that is invariant to isotropic scaling and orthogonal transformations.
main_functionalities: Compute similarities between latent representations at different layers

strengths: Good for comparing how representations evolve across depth
Stable summary metric (compared to raw cosine on single tokens)
limitations: Single-input estimate can be noisy; best with multiple inputs
CKA depends on token sampling and preprocessing choices

research_applications.used_in: Similarity of neural network representations revisited
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the 36 th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)
research_applications.note: Introduces the linear CKA measure for comparing neural network representations.

research_applications.used_in: Fine-tuned transformers show clusters of dimilar representations across layers
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the Fourth BlackboxNLP Workshop on Analyzing and Interpreting Neural Networks for NLP
research_applications.note: Uses Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) to measure representational similarity across layers in fine-tuned transformer models (e.g., RoBERTa, ALBERT).

research_applications.used_in: Ecco: An Open Source Library for the Explainability of Transformer Language Models
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the 59th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the 11th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing: System Demonstrations
research_applications.note: Introduces the Ecco toolkit for analyzing transformer language models. Includes implementation of CKA for comparing layer representations and studying representational similarity across model depth.

toolkits.name: Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF)

description.overview: Matrix factorization approaches such as non-negative matrix factorization decompose internal representations into a concise set of patterns.
main_functionalities: Summarizes latent representations (activations) with a small number of factors (features) that can be interpreted much more easily than individual neurons

strengths: Unlike several alternative matrix-factorization approaches, NMF enforces non-negativity, thus avoiding cancellation effects and highlighting semantic clusters
Enables discovery of human-interpretable features
Fast algorithms to compute NMF exist
limitations: Enforcing non-negative can result in information loss
Factors can be polysemantic
Assumes an additive structure for activations which may not hold in practice

research_applications.used_in: Ecco: An Open Source Library for the Explainability of Transformer Language Models
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the 59th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the 11th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing: System Demonstrations
research_applications.note: Introduces the Ecco toolkit for analyzing transformer language models. Includes implementation NMF for discovering features.

research_applications.used_in: Algorithms for Non-negative Matrix Factorization
research_applications.source: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 13: Proceedings of the 2000 Conference
research_applications.note: Introduces multiplicative update rules to compute NMF

research_applications.used_in: Decomposing MLP Activations into Interpretable Features via Semi-Nonnegative Matrix Factorization
research_applications.note: Proposes decomposing MLP activations with Semi-Nonnegative Matrix Factorization for finding interpretable features in the activations.

toolkits.name: Token Ranking Comparison

description.overview: Token Ranking Comparison tracks how a model ranks selected tokens at a specific prompt position, allowing comparison of token preference trajectories under the model’s next-token distribution.
main_functionalities: Inspect how token preference changes across layers

strengths: Gives an intuitive view of the model’s relative preference between specific hypotheses (tokens)
limitations: Can compare vacabulary tokens and not all words (without modifications)
Ranks are relative and do not directly convey probability mass differences

research_applications.used_in: Ecco: An Open Source Library for the Explainability of Transformer Language Models
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the 59th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the 11th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing: System Demonstrations
research_applications.note: Introduces Ecco and its interactive analysis tools, including token ranking inspection for transformer language models.

toolkits.name: Similarity-Based Explanations

description.overview: Explains a prediction by retrieving the most similar training examples, where similarity takes into account the model trained for a specific task.
main_functionalities: Finds top-k  inputs in training that are most similar (and optionally least similar) to a target test input

strengths: Produces example-based explanations that are intuitive and easy to inspect (nearest-neighbour style rationales)
Similarity is model-aware (based on how the model’s parameters would update), not just embedding distance
limitations: Can be computationally expensive for large models or large training sets

research_applications.used_in: Alibi Explain — Similarity-based explanations (documentation)
research_applications.note: Documents similarity explainers in Alibi, including Similarity-Based Explanations and its similarity metrics.

research_applications.used_in: Alibi Explain: Algorithms for Explaining Machine Learning Models
research_applications.note: Describes the Alibi library, which provides multiple explainers including similarity-based methods.

research_applications.used_in: Evaluation of Similarity-based Explanations
research_applications.note: Systematically evaluates similarity-based explanation methods and analyzes how well retrieved examples align with model behavior.

toolkits.name: CCA and SVCCA
toolkits.notes: Representation similarity across transformer layers using Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA).

description.overview: Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) is a statistical method that measures the similarity between two sets of variables by finding pairs of linear combinations—one from each set—that are maximally correlated. SVCCA is a variant that is fast and invariant to affine transforms
main_functionalities: Computes similarity of latent representations across transformer layers

strengths: Invariant to linear transformations of representation space
Widely used in representation analysis research
limitations: Can be numerically unstable without regularization

research_applications.used_in: Relations Between Two Sets of Variates
research_applications.note: Original introduction of Canonical Correlation Analysis by Hotelling.

research_applications.used_in: SVCCA: Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis for Deep Learning Dynamics and Interpretability
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the 31st Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
research_applications.note: Introduces SVCCA for analyzing representations in deep neural networks; foundational for representation similarity analysis in modern deep models.

research_applications.used_in: Insights on Representational Similarity in Neural Networks with Canonical Correlation
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the 31st Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
research_applications.note: Introduces Projection-Weighted CCA (PWCCA) and further analyzes representation similarity in deep networks.

research_applications.used_in: BERT is Not an Interlingua and the Bias of Tokenization
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the 2nd Workshop on Deep Learning Approaches for Low-Resource NLP
research_applications.note: Uses Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) to find that pretrained multilingual BERT does not learn a unified interlingual representation space. Instead, it partitions its internal representations by language.

research_applications.used_in: The Bottom-up Evolution of Representations in the Transformer: A Study with Machine Translation and Language Modeling Objectives
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the 2019 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing and the 9th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing (EMNLP-IJCNLP)
research_applications.note: Uses canonical correlation analysis to investigate how information flows across transformer layers and how the flow hinges on the objective adopted for learning.

research_applications.used_in: Similarity Analysis of Contextual Word Representation Models
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
research_applications.note: Uses canonical correlation analysis to measure the similarity between different latent representations.

research_applications.used_in: Ecco: An Open Source Library for the Explainability of Transformer Language Models
research_applications.note: Introduces the Ecco toolkit for analyzing transformer language models. Implements CCA and SVCCA to study representational similarity across layers.

toolkits.name: Distributed Alignment Search (DAS)
toolkits.notes: DAS trains one shared alignment (a rotation of a hidden layer) via gradient descent over a set of examples, so the alignment itself is learned at the task/dataset level (global), but the underlying causal test — an interchange intervention swapping in a source example's subspace activations — is defined and evaluated on individual base/source input pairs (local).

description.overview: DAS finds a linear subspace of a neural network's hidden representation that aligns with a hypothesized interpretable high-level causal variable. It optimizes an orthogonal (rotation) matrix via gradient descent so that 'distributed interchange interventions' on that subspace — rotating the representation into the new basis, swapping in values from a source input for the target subspace only, then rotating back — produce the same counterfactual behavior as interventions on the corresponding variable in a symbolic high-level causal model. Unlike prior 'localist' causal-abstraction approaches that search over which individual neurons encode a concept, DAS allows concepts to be encoded as linear combinations of neurons.
main_functionalities: Learns an orthogonal rotation matrix aligning disjoint subspaces of a layer's activations with variables of a hypothesized high-level causal model
Performs distributed interchange interventions and compares the resulting counterfactual output to the high-level causal model's prediction
Computes Interchange Intervention Accuracy (IIA) as a graded faithfulness metric for how well the alignment holds
Can be applied hierarchically ('Subspace DAS') to test whether an aligned subspace further decomposes into sub-representations

strengths: Finds alignments via gradient descent rather than the brute-force combinatorial search used by prior causal-abstraction methods, and empirically achieves higher IIA than both a brute-force search baseline and the closest localist alignment
Does not assume high-level variables map to disjoint groups of individual neurons, so it can find concepts distributed across neurons
Runtime is invariant to the number of alignment hypotheses tested, unlike brute-force search, whose cost explodes combinatorially
When interchange-intervention accuracy reaches 100%, this provides a formal guarantee, grounded in causal abstraction theory, that the identified causal structure is genuinely present in the model

Shown to reveal genuine internal structure: in one experiment, DAS found representations that could not be decomposed further into representations of individual entities, evidence the network implements an abstracted symbolic algorithm
Its scaled-up variant (Boundless DAS) shows alignments generalize robustly to unseen inputs, inserted irrelevant context, and alternate output formats
limitations: The original method still requires a manual search over the target subspace's dimensionality and location, which motivated a follow-up ('Boundless DAS') that learns the subspace size instead

Poor scalability to large models: the number of rotation-matrix parameters grows roughly with the square of representation size, becoming intractable for standard training infrastructure on large models
Requires a pre-specified (partial or complete) causal graph of the data-generating process, interchangeable high-level variables, and the ability to sample counterfactual base/source input pairs
Uses a linear (orthogonal) transformation, which may not be optimal if the aligning variable is represented on a non-linear sub-manifold
Gradient-descent optimization is not guaranteed to reach a global optimum, so multiple random seeds are typically run and the best result reported
A low interchange-intervention accuracy is not proof the causal structure is absent, since it could reflect a highly non-linear encoding that DAS's linear search misses
IIA is bounded by the underlying model's task accuracy, and can appear spuriously high in randomly-initialized networks, requiring random-baseline calibration checks

research_applications.used_in: Finding Alignments Between Interpretable Causal Variables and Distributed Neural Representations
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the Third Conference on Causal Learning and Reasoning (CLeaR)
research_applications.note: Introduces DAS.

research_applications.used_in: Causal Abstraction: A Theoretical Foundation for Mechanistic Interpretability
research_applications.note: Situates DAS within a broader causal-abstraction taxonomy as a 'modular feature learning' method and notes it has since been used to analyze causal mechanisms in a variety of deep learning models.

research_applications.used_in: Interpretability at Scale: Identifying Causal Mechanisms in Alpaca
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the 37th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
research_applications.note: Introduces Boundless DAS, which replaces DAS's remaining brute-force search over subspace dimensionality with learned boundary parameters, scaling DAS-style interchange interventions to a 7B-parameter instruction-tuned LLM.

research_applications.used_in: CausalGym: Benchmarking causal interpretability methods on linguistic tasks
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers)
research_applications.note: Benchmarks DAS alongside linear probing and other methods on a suite of linguistic tasks, finding DAS the most causally efficacious method tested, and uses it to study learning trajectories of two linguistic phenomena.

research_applications.used_in: MIB: A Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark
research_applications.source: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)
research_applications.note: Defines a causal-variable-localization benchmark track comparing featurization methods, including DAS and sparse autoencoders, finding that supervised DAS performs best among the methods tested.

research_applications.used_in: HyperDAS: Towards Automating Mechanistic Interpretability with Hypernetworks
research_applications.note: Extends DAS with a transformer-based hypernetwork that automates its brute-force search step, automatically locating token positions and constructing concept features.

research_applications.used_in: Model Alignment Search
research_applications.note: Introduces Model Alignment Search, described as a combination of model stitching and DAS, built on DAS's formulation to transfer causal information between two different neural networks rather than within a single model.

research_applications.used_in: Faithful Bi-Directional Model Steering via Distribution Matching and Distributed Interchange Interventions
research_applications.note: Builds on DAS's distributed interchange intervention mechanism, replacing its probability-maximization training objective with a distribution-matching objective to enable bi-directional, data-derived model steering.

research_applications.used_in: One mechanism for many mental spaces: a shared router over a value slot in language models
research_applications.note: Trains a subspace using DAS to causally control which discourse space (e.g., counterfactual, belief, fictional, temporal) a value belongs to, and extends it to train per-readout subspaces and test cross-type transfer.

toolkits.name: Activation Steering (ActAdd / CAA)

description.overview: Activation steering modifies a language model's internal activations at inference time using a direction associated with a behavior or concept. Activation Addition (ActAdd) constructs a steering vector from the difference between activations elicited by contrastive prompts and adds the vector to the residual stream. Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) uses differences from multiple contrastive examples to form a more robust steering direction.
main_functionalities: Construct a direction in activation space from contrastive prompts or examples
Intervene on intermediate activations to causally steer generated behavior
Compare model outputs before and after the activation intervention

strengths: ActAdd does not require optimization or a backward pass to construct the steering vector
Can produce a visible causal change in generation from a small number of contrastive examples
CAA can aggregate activation differences across multiple contrastive examples
limitations: Results depend on choices such as the layer, steering coefficient, and contrastive prompts or examples

research_applications.used_in: Steering Language Models With Activation Engineering
research_applications.note: Introduces Activation Addition (ActAdd), an inference-time activation engineering method based on contrastive prompt activation differences.

research_applications.used_in: Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition
research_applications.note: Introduces Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), which averages contrastive activation differences across examples to obtain steering directions.

toolkits.name: Attention-Head Ablation / Knockout

description.overview: Attention-head ablation evaluates the contribution or necessity of an attention head by disabling its output and measuring the resulting change in model behavior or task performance.
main_functionalities: Disable individual attention heads or groups of heads
Measure the change in model outputs or task metrics after ablation
Study redundancy and necessity of attention components

strengths: Provides a direct intervention on a specific model component
Can reveal substantial redundancy among attention heads
limitations: The measured effect is specific to the chosen ablation intervention and evaluation metric

research_applications.used_in: Are Sixteen Heads Really Better than One?
research_applications.note: Systematically analyzes the effect of removing attention heads and reports substantial redundancy in multi-head attention.

toolkits.name: Tuned Lens

description.overview: The Tuned Lens decodes intermediate transformer hidden states into vocabulary distributions using a learned affine translator for each layer of a frozen language model. It is designed as a refinement of the Logit Lens.
main_functionalities: Decode hidden states at each transformer layer into a distribution over the vocabulary
Track how latent next-token predictions evolve layer by layer
Compare intermediate predictions with the model's final prediction

strengths: Reported to be more predictive, reliable, and unbiased than the Logit Lens
Provides a layer-wise view of how model predictions are refined
limitations: Requires training an affine probe or translator for each transformer block

research_applications.used_in: Eliciting Latent Predictions from Transformers with the Tuned Lens
research_applications.note: Introduces the Tuned Lens and evaluates it on autoregressive language models up to 20B parameters.

toolkits.name: Patchscopes

description.overview: Patchscopes is a framework for inspecting hidden representations by taking a representation from a source computation and patching it into a target computation constructed to reveal information encoded in that representation.
main_functionalities: Extract a hidden representation from a source prompt and layer
Patch the representation into a chosen position and layer of a target prompt
Use the target computation to decode or inspect information in the source representation

strengths: Unifies multiple representation-inspection techniques under a common patching framework
Can use a language model's own generation behavior to produce interpretable readouts of internal states
limitations: The interpretation can depend on the design of the target prompt, target layer, and target computation

research_applications.used_in: Patchscopes: A Unifying Framework for Inspecting Hidden Representations of Language Models
research_applications.note: Introduces Patchscopes as a general framework for inspecting language-model hidden representations through representation patching.

toolkits.name: Causal Tracing

description.overview: Causal tracing localizes internal states involved in a model behavior by comparing a clean run, a corrupted run that suppresses the behavior, and restoration runs in which selected clean activations are reintroduced into the corrupted computation.
main_functionalities: Create a corrupted computation in which a target behavior is degraded
Restore selected clean hidden states or components into the corrupted run
Measure the recovery of the target output to localize causally important states

strengths: Uses explicit interventions to localize internal states that causally restore a behavior
Provides position-by-layer maps of where information relevant to a factual prediction is processed
limitations: Results depend on the corruption procedure, restoration intervention, and chosen behavioral metric

research_applications.used_in: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
research_applications.note: Introduces causal tracing to identify internal states involved in factual recall before applying the ROME editing method.

toolkits.name: Input Marginalization

description.overview: Input Marginalization estimates token importance by marginalizing a token over contextually plausible replacements rather than erasing it with a fixed value. The method was proposed to reduce the out-of-distribution problem caused by token erasure.
main_functionalities: Estimate context-dependent replacement probabilities for an input token
Marginalize the target model prediction over plausible replacements
Compute token-level importance from the change in prediction after marginalization

strengths: Designed to address out-of-distribution perturbations produced by zero or fixed-value token erasure
limitations: A later evaluation found no evidence that Input Marginalization consistently outperforms a Leave-One-Out baseline and identified failure cases for highly predictable words

research_applications.used_in: Interpretation of NLP models through input marginalization
research_applications.note: Introduces Input Marginalization for sentiment analysis and natural language inference.

research_applications.used_in: Double Trouble: How to not Explain a Text Classifier’s Decisions Using Counterfactuals Synthesized by Masked Language Models?
research_applications.note: Re-evaluates Input Marginalization and reports limitations relative to Leave-One-Out.

toolkits.name: TCAV (Testing with Concept Activation Vectors)

description.overview: TCAV evaluates model sensitivity to a human-defined concept by learning a Concept Activation Vector (CAV) from examples of that concept and measuring directional derivatives of the model output along the concept direction.
main_functionalities: Learn a concept direction from user-provided concept examples and comparison examples
Measure directional sensitivity of a target output to the learned concept direction
Aggregate concept sensitivity into a quantitative TCAV score

strengths: Provides explanations in terms of human-defined concepts rather than individual input features
Supports statistical testing across multiple concept and random-control sets
limitations: Results depend on the examples used to define the concept and the comparison or random-control sets

research_applications.used_in: Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV)
research_applications.note: Introduces TCAV for quantitative concept-based interpretation.

toolkits.name: Knowledge Neurons

description.overview: Knowledge Neurons identifies feed-forward network neurons associated with factual knowledge by attributing a model's factual prediction to internal neuron activations and aggregating evidence across prompts expressing the same fact.
main_functionalities: Compute attribution scores for internal feed-forward neurons with respect to a factual prediction
Identify neurons that consistently contribute across prompts expressing the same knowledge
Validate identified neurons through activation interventions

strengths: Targets internal feed-forward neurons rather than only input tokens
Uses multiple prompts for the same fact to identify consistently associated neurons
limitations: The identified neurons are tied to the tested factual relations and prompting setup

research_applications.used_in: Knowledge Neurons in Pretrained Transformers
research_applications.note: Introduces Knowledge Neurons for locating factual knowledge in pretrained transformers.

toolkits.name: Observable Propagation (ObProp)

description.overview: Observable Propagation (ObProp) is a method for finding linear feature vectors used by transformer language models in a task. It starts from an observable, a linear functional associated with a task, and propagates it through the model to uncover internal feature vectors.
main_functionalities: Define an observable corresponding to a model task or output property
Propagate the observable to derive internal linear feature vectors
Compare discovered feature vectors using a coupling coefficient

strengths: Designed to find useful feature vectors using almost no labeled data
Can be used to investigate internal features associated with bias and task behavior
limitations: The framework focuses on linear observables and linear feature vectors

research_applications.used_in: Observable Propagation: Uncovering Feature Vectors in Transformers
research_applications.note: Introduces ObProp and evaluates it on occupational gender bias, political party prediction, and programming-language detection.

toolkits.name: LEACE / Concept Scrubbing

description.overview: LEACE (LEAst-squares Concept Erasure) removes a specified concept from a representation in closed form while minimizing changes to the representation. Concept scrubbing applies concept erasure across model layers to study whether a model behavior relies on linearly decodable concept information.
main_functionalities: Compute a closed-form transformation that erases linearly decodable concept information
Apply concept erasure to hidden representations
Scrub a concept across multiple layers and measure resulting changes in model behavior

strengths: Provably prevents all linear classifiers from detecting the erased concept
Uses a closed-form solution
Provides an intervention for testing reliance on linearly represented concepts
limitations: The guarantee concerns linear classifiers and therefore does not establish removal of all possible nonlinear concept information

research_applications.used_in: LEACE: Perfect linear concept erasure in closed form
research_applications.note: Introduces LEACE and applies a multi-layer procedure called concept scrubbing to language models.

toolkits.name: Causal Mediation Analysis

description.overview: Causal Mediation Analysis interprets model behavior by treating internal components such as neurons or attention heads as mediators between an input intervention and an output effect. It decomposes behavior into direct and mediated causal effects.
main_functionalities: Define an input treatment and an output outcome
Intervene on internal mediators such as neurons or attention heads
Estimate direct and indirect causal effects through model components

strengths: Connects internal model structure with behavior through explicit causal interventions
Can quantify how much of an observed effect is mediated by specific internal components
limitations: Requires defining meaningful treatments, mediators, interventions, and outcome measures

research_applications.used_in: Causal Mediation Analysis for Interpreting Neural NLP: The Case of Gender Bias
research_applications.note: Applies causal mediation analysis to neurons and attention heads in pretrained Transformer language models to study gender bias.

toolkits.name: Automated Neuron Explanations

description.overview: Automated neuron explanation methods use a language model to generate natural-language hypotheses describing the behavior of internal neurons from examples of their activations, and then score those explanations by how well they predict neuron activations on new text.
main_functionalities: Collect text examples and activation patterns for an internal neuron
Generate a natural-language explanation of the neuron's behavior
Score the explanation by using it to predict activations on additional examples

strengths: Scales semantic labeling beyond manual inspection of individual neurons
Includes an explicit scoring stage for evaluating generated explanations
limitations: The released explanations and scores are imperfect, and many neurons remain difficult to explain accurately

research_applications.used_in: Language models can explain neurons in language models
research_applications.note: Uses GPT-4 to generate and score explanations for neurons in GPT-2 and releases the resulting dataset.

toolkits.name: Integrated Hessians

description.overview: Integrated Hessians extends Integrated Gradients from individual feature attribution to pairwise feature interactions by integrating second-order derivative information along a path from a baseline to the input.
main_functionalities: Compute pairwise feature-interaction attribution scores
Produce an interaction matrix showing which feature pairs jointly influence a prediction
Extend path-based attribution from first-order importance to second-order interactions

strengths: Provides an axiomatic method for explaining pairwise feature interactions
Is not restricted to a specific neural-network architecture or model class
limitations: Focuses on pairwise interactions rather than arbitrary higher-order interactions

research_applications.used_in: Explaining Explanations: Axiomatic Feature Interactions for Deep Networks
research_applications.note: Introduces Integrated Hessians as an extension of Integrated Gradients for pairwise feature interactions.

toolkits.name: Future Lens

description.overview: Future Lens analyzes whether a single hidden state contains information about tokens that will be generated several positions later. The method uses linear approximation and causal intervention techniques to decode or test future-token information from intermediate states.
main_functionalities: Predict future hidden states or token distributions from a single current hidden state
Test future-token information with causal transplantation of hidden states across contexts
Visualize information about tokens multiple steps ahead

strengths: Extends intermediate-state decoding beyond the immediate next-token prediction
Combines predictive readouts with causal intervention experiments
limitations: The reported experiments are centered on GPT-J-6B and require fitted mappings or prompts for some readout variants

research_applications.used_in: Future Lens: Anticipating Subsequent Tokens from a Single Hidden State
research_applications.note: Introduces Future Lens and studies future-token information in hidden states of GPT-J-6B.

toolkits.name: Information Bottleneck Attribution

description.overview: Information Bottleneck Attribution inserts a learned information bottleneck into transformer representations and optimizes it to retain information needed for a prediction while suppressing less relevant information, yielding feature attributions and layer-wise insight into information flow.
main_functionalities: Insert an information bottleneck into transformer representations
Optimize the bottleneck to preserve prediction-relevant information
Derive feature-level attributions and inspect how information changes across layers

strengths: Provides both feature attribution and analysis of information flow through transformer layers
Reported to outperform two competing attribution methods in degradation tests on four datasets

research_applications.used_in: Inserting Information Bottlenecks for Attribution in Transformers
research_applications.note: Introduces information-bottleneck attribution for transformer models using BERT as the main example.

toolkits.name: TRAK

description.overview: TRAK (Tracing with the Randomly-projected After Kernel) is a training-data attribution method that assigns influence scores from training examples to model predictions using gradient-derived features and random projections.
main_functionalities: Trace a model prediction back to influential training examples
Construct scalable gradient-based features using random projections
Compute data-attribution scores for large differentiable models

strengths: Designed to be both effective and computationally tractable at large scale
Can match methods that require training thousands of models while using only a handful of trained models
Demonstrated on language models including BERT and mT5
limitations: Requires access to training data and gradient information, and the method uses multiple trained models in its attribution pipeline

research_applications.used_in: TRAK: Attributing Model Behavior at Scale
research_applications.note: Introduces TRAK for scalable training-data attribution and evaluates it across vision, vision-language, and language models.

toolkits.name: Influence Functions

description.overview: Influence Functions estimate how a model prediction or test loss would change if a particular training example were infinitesimally upweighted or removed, using gradients and inverse-Hessian-vector products instead of retraining the model from scratch for each example.
main_functionalities: Estimate the influence of individual training examples on a test prediction or loss
Approximate the effect of upweighting or removing training examples
Identify training examples responsible for model errors or behavior

strengths: Provides a principled approximation to leave-one-out retraining effects without retraining once per training example
Can be used to trace predictions and errors back to influential training data
limitations: Requires gradient and second-order information and relies on approximating inverse-Hessian-vector products
The classical formulation is challenging for large, non-convex neural networks

research_applications.used_in: Understanding Black-box Predictions via Influence Functions
research_applications.note: Introduces the modern use of influence functions for tracing model predictions back to training examples.
